passage:
"Kashish, let me tell you why I frowned at the message you showed me," said Avni. "When I was twenty-four, a stranger in a chat offered me an easy work-from-home job: rate videos, earn a fixed amount for each one. All I had to do was pay a small deposit to activate my account. It felt harmless, and the first payout even reached my bank.

"Then I got greedy. They said bigger deposits paid more, so I put in more. The account froze, and the stranger vanished. Only afterwards did I ask the question I should have asked first: why would anyone give away money for clicking? I never checked whether the company was registered.

"Now, when anyone offers money for almost no work, I ask that question before anything else. And I never pay in order to earn."

qa.q: What did the stranger ask Avni to pay to activate the account?
qa.a: The stranger asked for a small deposit.

qa.q: Why did Avni put in more money after the first payout?
qa.a: The first payout made the offer feel real and touched Avni's hope, and greed followed when the stranger said bigger deposits paid more.

qa.q: What should Kashish check before replying to an offer like this?
qa.a: Ask why a stranger would give money away, check whether the company is registered, and never pay in order to earn.

qa.q: How might the stranger have seen the young Avni?
qa.a: As a hopeful person who could be drawn in with a small payout and then pushed to deposit more.

grounding: An easy remote-job offer works on Avni's hope and greed; Avni is left with the lesson to ask why a stranger would give money away and never pay to earn.

passage:
"Alka, look at this! A remote job. Just like videos and rate restaurants. Eight hundred a task!"
"Who sent it?"
"A woman called Neha on a chat app. She said I was selected."
"Selected from what? Did you apply?"
Aditi paused. "No. But the first two tasks paid. Look, the money came."
"And now?"
"Now I have to deposit five thousand to unlock the 'premium tasks'. Then I earn triple."
Alka put down her tea. "Aditi, why would a stranger pay you eight hundred to like a video?"
"...To hook me?"
"Exactly. They pay small, then ask for big. Real jobs don't make you pay to earn. What's the company's name?"
Aditi searched it. No registration. No website. Just the chat group. Her stomach sank. She had so wanted it to be real.
"Too good to be true," she said quietly, and blocked Neha's number.

qa.q: How much did Aditi have to deposit to unlock the premium tasks?
What was Aditi feeling when she searched the company and found nothing?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and uneasy, her stomach sinking, because she had so wanted the job to be real.

qa.q: What questions helped Aditi see the trap?
qa.a: Why a stranger would pay her to like videos, whether she had applied, and whether the company was registered, plus the fact that real jobs don't make you pay to earn.

qa.q: How might Alka see the offer from the start?
qa.a: Alka is suspicious and protective, seeing the small early payments as a hook before a bigger demand.

grounding: A remote-job scam plays on hope with small early payouts; the protagonist asks why a stranger would pay, checks registration and refuses to pay to earn.

passage:
I'm Bhupen, and last winter a man I'd met in an online chess group started telling me about his "crypto arbitrage". He was friendly, sent me screenshots, said my money would double in sixty days. I'd had a bad year. The idea of doubling felt like a door opening.
I told my friend Sangeeta about it over chai. She didn't laugh. She just asked, "Why would he share a secret that makes money for free?" I didn't have an answer.
That night I looked up the platform he recommended. It wasn't registered with any regulator I could find. Its website was two months old. The "reviews" all used the same sentences.
Looking back, what hooked me wasn't greed exactly. It was hope. I wanted something to go right. That's what the scam was built on. I stopped replying to him, reported his profile to the group admins, and told Sangeeta she'd probably saved me a lot.

qa.q: How long was the platform's website, according to Bhupen?
What made Bhupen want to believe the offer?
qa.a: Bhupen felt hopeful after a bad year, and the idea of doubling money felt like a door opening.

qa.q: How did Bhupen check the offer?
qa.a: Bhupen asked why a stranger would share free money, looked for the platform's registration, and noticed the website was new and the reviews repeated.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta see her own question afterwards?
qa.a: Sangeeta may feel relieved and glad that one simple question helped Bhupen step back.

grounding: An offer of double returns works on hope; the protagonist asks why a stranger would give money away, checks registration and treats it as a trap.
